Someone will correct me if I'm wrong but I think the days of mandatory disk partitioning are over, or at least on Ubuntu/Debian derivatives for desktops. The default works without issue for me.
Until something fill up your disk and you're fucked as you can't log in anymore. There is are reasons why the veterans used to partition the disks the way they did.

We used to do this on servers because it helped with read/write speed. Disk access was slow, RAM was in short supply, so partitioning created a swap space for what RAM couldn't hold and put key disk partitions near the center so read speeds were faster. The downside was the moment a key partition (like /var) filled, the OS and application froze.

Now disks are faster and we often have more available RAM than an OS needs. Best leave the OS to dynamically allocate as needed lest something too small fill up. Most distros now are better about keeping boot partitions from filling. They just do better cleanup after kernel updates.

Unless you want to use more than one disk, in which case the default is useless. It only sets up a generic Boot/Swap/Root scheme.

Put it this way, the default is a cookie cutter and i'm baking a cake.

That is a horrible partition scheme.

For starters, I can't mention btrfs because I don't use it. Last time I tried it my boot times were +30 seconds from grub. It was probably Ubuntu's fault, but whatever. My current set up is ideal for me.

500 MB for /boot/efi is way too much. That partition only uses just under 4 MB.

Swap is fine.

I would also make a 5GB partition for /boot.

This is where I would do things differently.

Let's just say you have 100 GB left on /dev/sda. I know it's more, but the journal will take some, plus, it's not actually 120 GB.

I would make 2 partitions at 50 GB each. I will explain why later.

Then, for /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc, I would make them a logical volume and combine them to give you 1TB for your /home. The best part of this is that if you run out of space, attach another drive, attach it to the volume group, expand the lv and you now have more storage. And then, everything goes in your $HOME directory.

Now, about the two 50 GB partitions. This is my own little trick to make life easy. Assuming you have /boot/efi, /boot, and SWAP, you would be left with /dev/sda3 and /dev/sda4. When you install your distro, it will be installed on /dev/sda3. Now, lets say you want to try out a new distro, you install that new distro on /dev/sda4. Both will use your LVM mounted /home for your home directory, so all your data is safe. This allows you to easily distro hop. Or, if you are like me, you can do fresh installed with each new release instead of doing dist-upgrade.

1) I do not see a problem with having two drives at different speeds. You may notice slow downs if you are trying to access something on the 5200 drive. And there is no real way to determine which is on the 5200 and which is on the 7400, though it is safe to assume that files are written sequentially.

2) Keep in mind that /boot/efi is required to be its own partition because it needs to be vfat (fucking microsoft). The files on that partition are only a few megs in size. The reason /boot is so large is because when you do your updates, older kernels are not being removed. It's generally a good idea to keep the previous 2 kernels in case a new one borks something. You can go ahead and delete the older kernels.

3) While I can understand the wanting for putting heavily used files on your SSD for speed of access, unless you have enough storage, I do not see a benefit. Especially, once you start doing this it becomes a management nightmare. Let Steam use its default. Let WINE use its defaults. Once you start having to manually specify mount points like this, it becomes a nightmare when it comes time to update the distro or needing to do a fresh install of Steam or something.

The benefits gained do not outweigh the inconvenience.

With that said, I would accomplish your goals like this:

(I write disk rather than SATA port)

1) Install to disk1. Login to the system so that all the files that need to be in /home/USER are created.

2) Create partition on disk3 and copy over all the data that you want to keep.

3) After you are 100% sure your data is stored on that drive and isn't corrupted...reformat/partition drive #2.

4) Copy all files from your /home/USER to the partition on disk2. This will require mounting the drive, a good place would be /mnt/home. Be sure to copy the hidden files that begin with a .

5) Delete the /home/USER directory and create a symlink directory at /home/USER that points to disk2 https://www.nixtutor.com/freebsd/understanding-symbolic-links/. NOTE: You will likely have to modify your fstab config file to automatically mount your disks upon boot. I would set something up so it would look like /dev/sdb mounts to /mnt/home and /dev/sdc mounts to /mnt/music The /home/USER symlink would point to /mnt/home

6) Inside /home/USER (which is now on disk2 mounted at /mnt/home) do another symlink that points from /home/USER/Music to /mnt/music

7) Copy your non music files back to disk2.

8) Profit
